clue.text: Son married English nationalist in European country

parts.note: S is the short form of son on a form or a family tree
wed is the headline word for married
E is the standard short form of English
N is the label a nationalist candidate carries on a British election result

explanation.surface: A line from a dossier on a man with a wife and strong patriotic views.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces run straight on with nothing to mark where one ends and the next begins, and three of them are single letters. The surface hands you a plausible person to distract from that.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a country in northern Europe, so the definition is simply the class it belongs to.

clue.text: It's said you and I have to mingle

indicators.note: 'It's said' points at how the words sound when spoken rather than at how they are spelt.

parts.note: you and I together are WE, and WE HAVE spoken at speed collapses into one word

explanation.surface: One half of a couple grumbling that they are both obliged to socialise.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'we have' loses its aitch and runs together, which is the whole of the wordplay. The obligation the surface complains about belongs to no part of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Threads that weave pass in and out of each other, and to weave through a crowd is to mingle among it in the same way.

clue.text: Declines operation in doctor's

indicators.note: One thing in another is written inside it, so the letters before 'in' go within the word that follows.

parts.note: doctor shortens to DR and the possessive S is taken as a letter too
OP is the hospital short form of operation

explanation.surface: A patient turning surgery down at the doctor's.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'doctor's' is not doing grammar: its S is one of the letters wanted. Declines here is what a temperature does, not what a patient does.
explanation.definitionFit: When a price or a temperature drops it declines, the same downward movement said in a plainer word.

clue.text: West African beginning to bid for victory over East African capital

indicators.note: 'For' marks an exchange, one thing handed across in place of another, so a letter is swapped rather than added.
Something turned over lies the other way round, so the letters are read back to front.

parts.note: an Ivorian, from Cote d'Ivoire on the Gulf of Guinea, is a West African
the beginning of BID, and the letter that arrives
V for victory, Churchill's wartime sign, and the letter that leaves

explanation.surface: A West African side opening the bidding to win, against an East African capital.
explanation.walkthrough: V for victory is what makes the exchange work, and B arrives from the front of 'bid'. Once the swap is made the whole string is turned over, which is what 'over' is for in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenya's seat of government has been in Nairobi since the town grew up round a railway depot in 1899, and Kenya sits on Africa's eastern coast.

clue.text: Beyond sick, ultimately crave medicated sweet

parts.note: a house beyond the church is past it
ill is the plain word for sick

indicators.note: What comes ultimately is what comes last, so only the final letter of the word after it is wanted.

parts.note: the last letter of CRAVE

explanation.surface: Someone so unwell they are past wanting anything, craving one last thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beyond sick' reads as a single phrase meaning desperately unwell, and that is exactly the join the setter wants hidden: the two words belong to different pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is the small lozenge sucked for a sore throat, a sweet sold with medicine in it.

clue.text: Pressure to relax before playing City

indicators.note: What comes before something is written ahead of it, which settles which of the two pieces is put down first.

parts.note: P is the scientific symbol for pressure
to rest is to relax
a show that is playing is on

explanation.surface: A manager telling his side to unwind before a fixture against City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' is capitalised to look like the opposition in a fixture list when it is only the ordinary noun. The local club is Preston North End, which is what lets the football surface stand up.
explanation.definitionFit: Preston is a city in Lancashire, in the north-west of England, given city status in 2002.

clue.text: Bit of sentimentality from left-winger for fungal disease

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a piece of it, and the smallest piece a setter can mean is the letter it opens with.

parts.note: the opening letter of SENTIMENTALITY
from and of both say where a thing came out of, as in a man from Kent or of Kent
a Trot is a Trotskyist, British shorthand for anyone on the hard left

explanation.surface: A trace of soppiness showing up in a hard-line political activist.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words of the answer break in the wrong place: the political piece straddles the gap between them. 'From' looks like joining language and is doing letter work.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft rot is the disease that reduces a stored potato or carrot to mush, one of the standard rots of crops in store.

clue.text: Stubborn, loses information on the way

indicators.note: What a word loses is taken out of it, and the letters left close up in the order they already had.

parts.note: an intransigent negotiator refuses to shift, which is stubborn
gen is British informal for the information you need, out of 'general information'

explanation.surface: A stubborn traveller mislaying the facts somewhere along the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters lift out from inside the long word and what is left closes up, putting the word break somewhere it never was. 'Stubborn' opens the clue looking like the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A parcel in transit is still travelling and has not arrived, which is what 'on the way' says of it.

clue.text: Made fun of escape from Alcatraz number two by Scottish hooligan

parts.note: a prisoner on the lam has escaped and is still running; the lam is the flight itself
number two is the nursery phrase for what POO names plainly
ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan, the Glasgow word for a yob

explanation.surface: A jailbreak sequel with a couple of unsavoury characters in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Alcatraz contributes no letters; it is there so that 'escape' reads as part of a film title. The three pieces are American slang, nursery language and Glasgow slang in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To lampoon someone is to mock them in print or on stage, so 'made fun of' is the past tense of exactly that.

clue.text: Sloe gin, a volatile, flammable liquid

indicators.note: Something volatile will not hold still, so the letters described that way will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
the article taken as an eighth letter of fodder

explanation.surface: A tasting note on a bottle of homemade sloe gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volatile' works in both readings at once: a description of the drink in the surface, an instruction underneath it. Petrol is volatile in the chemist's sense as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasoline is the American word for petrol, a liquid that catches light readily.

clue.text: In the morning, sex with a female knocked over Catholic shrine

indicators.note: Something knocked over ends up the other way up, so those letters are read backwards.

parts.note: AM marks the hours before noon
IT is the coy old word for sex, the one behind the It girl
the article taken as a single letter
F is the standard short form of female on any form

explanation.surface: A morning tryst that ends with someone sent flying.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex is a survival from the 1920s and one of the small conventions worth banking. All four pieces are built facing one way and the whole lot is then turned round bodily.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatima is the Portuguese town where three shepherd children reported visions of the Virgin in 1917, now one of the most visited Catholic shrines anywhere.

clue.text: Toy weapon upset OAP, so there!

indicators.note: To upset something is to tip it over and spill it, leaving what was in it in no particular order.

parts.note: three letters of fodder
seven more letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A child annoying a pensioner and then crowing about it.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is the British label for an old age pensioner, the one printed on a bus pass. 'So there!' is the playground taunt, and its letters are wanted as much as the abbreviation's.
explanation.definitionFit: A peashooter is the tube a child blows dried peas through, a weapon only in the playground sense.

clue.text: A practice exam delivered in a frenzy

indicators.note: A line is delivered out loud, so what counts is how the words sound and not how they are written.

parts.note: a mock is the rehearsal exam British pupils sit before the real one, and 'a mock' spoken is the answer

explanation.surface: An exam paper being handed out to a panicking class.
explanation.walkthrough: Mocks are the practice papers sat in the spring before the summer exams, so the surface is a school corridor. Spoken, the article and the noun run together and shed a letter on the way.
explanation.definitionFit: To run amok is to rush about in a violent frenzy, so the answer is what 'in a frenzy' describes.

clue.text: Leather shoe with hole in losing mass, in time

indicators.note: A shoe with a hole in it has that hole inside it, so the letter goes within the word rather than beside it.
What a word is losing drops out of it, and the letters that remain close up.

parts.note: a moccasin is the soft leather shoe of the North American plains
a hole is drawn as a round O
M is the physics symbol for mass, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A worn shoe with the sole gone, growing lighter as it falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: A letter leaves the front of the shoe and another arrives near the back, two operations landing on the one word. 'In time' reads as a phrase, but the definition is only its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: An occasion is a particular time something happens, so 'on one occasion' and 'at one time' say the same thing.

clue.text: Piece of pork joint in cola originally tasted amazing

indicators.note: What sits in something goes inside it, so the letters named before 'in' are planted within what follows.

parts.note: the drink written straight out

indicators.note: What a word is originally is how it starts, so only the opening letter of each word here is taken.

parts.note: the opening letters of TASTED and AMAZING
the hip is a joint of the body, not of meat

explanation.surface: A cheap cola marinade that turned out far better than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' is the trap: there is pork in the clue, so the butcher's sense arrives first and the anatomical one is what the wordplay wants. The insertion lands after a single letter, which is an awkward place to look for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipolata is the small thin sausage served at Christmas, pork in a short length of skin.

clue.text: Article on number visiting a lake during pregnancy

definitions.note: 'During pregnancy' says when the answer applies rather than offering a word for it; antenatal is the adjective for anything happening in that stretch of time.

indicators.note: In a down clue what sits on something else is written above it, so the article is put down first.

parts.note: AN is one of the three English articles
ten is a number written out in full
someone visiting the neighbours is at the neighbours
the article taken as a single letter
L is the map abbreviation for lake, as in L Windermere

explanation.surface: A magazine piece about a trip to a lake while expecting.
explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces in a row, four of them tiny, and nothing to mark where the joins fall. 'Visiting' is the hardest of them: it is a preposition in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Antenatal means before the birth, so an antenatal class or check-up is one that happens while the baby is still on the way.

clue.text: Some artisan elderflower tea

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and that part is a run of consecutive letters.

parts.note: the run starts in the middle of ARTISAN and finishes on the first letter of ELDERFLOWER

explanation.surface: A cafe menu offering a fashionable herbal infusion.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden words are hardest to spot when the surface makes perfect sense on its own, and an artisan elderflower tea is exactly what a cafe would sell. The word break falls inside the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is a herbal infusion - camomile, mint, elderflower - drunk like tea but made without any tea leaves.

clue.text: Being stroppy, regularly avoided clowns here

definitions.note: 'Clowns here' points at the place instead of naming it, which is fair when the answer is somewhere clowns are always to be found.

indicators.note: What happens regularly happens at even intervals, and those evenly numbered letters are the ones avoided, leaving the first, third, fifth and so on.

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth and eleventh letters of BEING STROPPY

explanation.surface: Someone in a sulk being ticked off for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' usually collects letters; here it names the ones to throw away, and the count runs from the very first letter of all. The six survivors take no notice of the space between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The big top is the main circus tent, the one with the ring, the trapeze and the clowns in it.

clue.text: Choose the French World Cup hero?

definitions.note: The answer is a dog's name rather than a word for a hero, and the question mark admits it: one particular hero is meant.

parts.note: to pick is to choose
the French word for 'the' in front of a plural noun is LES

explanation.surface: A French footballer singled out as the star of a World Cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' is the usual way of asking for a French word rather than for French people. Pickles was the mongrel who found the stolen Jules Rimet trophy under a hedge in south London in 1966.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickles is the dog that sniffed out the stolen World Cup trophy weeks before the 1966 tournament, and was a national celebrity in Britain for it.

clue.text: Very drunk and impolite, lacking bit of refinement, in isolation

indicators.note: A word lacking something has it taken away, and what is left closes up.
A bit of a word is the smallest piece of it there is, the letter it begins with.

parts.note: so tired and very tired say the same thing
lit, or lit up, is old slang for drunk
rude is the plain word for impolite
the opening letter of REFINEMENT, and the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A drunk behaving badly at a party and ending the night alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very drunk' reads as one idea and is in fact two separate pieces, which is where the clue hides its join. LIT for drunk comes from lit up.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitude is the state of being on your own, which is what isolation names when it is chosen rather than imposed.

clue.text: Drunk bride's welcoming a shag?

definitions.note: A shag is one particular seabird rather than seabirds in general, and the question mark is the setter's admission that an example is standing in for its whole class.

indicators.note: Someone drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters described that way will not stay in the order printed.
A word welcoming something takes it in, so the letter that follows joins the ones being rearranged.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, apostrophe ignored
the article taken in as a seventh letter of fodder

explanation.surface: A tipsy bride at her own reception, fielding an indelicate question.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are the bride's own plus the one she takes in, seven in all. A shag is a cormorant-like diving bird of British coasts, which is the sense the question mark is guarding.
explanation.definitionFit: A shag is a green-black bird that nests on British sea cliffs, so the answer is the wider class it belongs to.

clue.text: I'm a match for Satan?

definitions.meaning: the Victorian friction match, the one in the old song about lighting your fag while you pack up your troubles
the name the fallen angel carried before his fall, used of the devil ever since

explanation.surface: Someone boasting that they can hold their own against the devil himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is speaking: 'I'm' tells you the two halves describe the same thing rather than compare two things. Read the surface way, 'a match for' means an equal, which is the whole disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucifer is the old name for a friction match, and Lucifer is the fallen angel the Bible names as Satan.

clue.text: I put on clothes to murder

indicators.note: To clothe a thing is to wrap something round it, so the word acting here goes outside the letter in front of it.

parts.note: to don a coat is to put it on
the pronoun taken as the letter it is

explanation.surface: Getting dressed of a morning with murder on the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is a verb here, not the things in the wardrobe, and 'put on' is the noun-free sense of donning. Four words of clue and every one of them is working.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone in is to kill them, the blunt informal phrase a thriller uses for murder.

clue.text: With luck, revolution repelled minister

indicators.note: Something repelled is driven back the way it came, so those letters are written in reverse.

parts.note: with luck and by chance say the same thing, and the noun behind it is CHANCE
one complete revolution is a roll, and ROLL driven back reads LLOR

explanation.surface: A minister who luckily sees off an attempted uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: A revolution is one turn of a wheel before it is anything political, and that is the sense wanted. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is the minister who runs the British Treasury.
explanation.definitionFit: A chancellor is a minister of state, and in Britain the Chancellor of the Exchequer is the one in charge of the nation's money.

clue.text: Large gold robbery cleared out truck

parts.note: L is the clothing-label short form of large
OR is gold in heraldry, the tincture on a coat of arms

indicators.note: A word cleared out has had its insides taken away, so only the letters at either end survive.

parts.note: the first and last letters of ROBBERY

explanation.surface: A big gold heist that left the place stripped bare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleared out' sounds like what a robbery does to a vault and is aimed instead at the word ROBBERY itself. OR for gold comes from heraldry and is worth owning early.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry is what the British call a truck, the same large goods vehicle under two names.

clue.text: Old men are going hungry, initially, in Irish town

indicators.note: Taken initially, each word offers only the letter it starts with.

parts.note: the opening letters of the five words in order

explanation.surface: Pensioners going without meals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' arrives after the words it governs, so all five are in play rather than just the one beside it. Omagh is the county town of Tyrone, in Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Omagh is a market town in County Tyrone, on the island of Ireland.

clue.text: Coach agreed to back political alliance

indicators.note: Sent back, letters are written in the opposite direction to the one they came in.

parts.note: a railway coach is a car, as in the dining car
to agree to a thing is to let it happen, and LET sent back reads TEL

explanation.surface: A coach agreeing to support a political grouping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' offers a bus, a trainer and a railway carriage, and only the last of them gives three letters. The Cartel des Gauches was a bloc of French left parties in the 1920s, which is the political sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartel is a combination of parties or firms acting as one bloc, so a grouping of parties formed to act together is a cartel.

clue.text: Deduce northern Alabama is hellish

parts.note: to infer is to deduce from what you have
N is the compass short form of northern
AL is the postal abbreviation for Alabama

explanation.surface: A verdict on the northern end of a southern state.
explanation.walkthrough: American state abbreviations run to two letters and turn up constantly in British puzzles; AL is Alabama's. 'Deduce' opens the clue in the position a definition usually takes.
explanation.definitionFit: Infernal means belonging to the inferno, so 'hellish' is its literal sense, the one it had before it weakened into mere annoyance.

clue.text: Ring American editor experiencing tough patch

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them
US stands in for anything American
ED is the masthead short form of editor

explanation.surface: A phone call from an editor in the States during a difficult spell.
explanation.walkthrough: A tough patch here is not a bad week but a hardened area of skin, and 'experiencing' is what turns the phrase adjectival. Ring is the British telephone verb, not anything circular.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin that is callused has grown hard pads where it is rubbed, so it is carrying a tough patch in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Original characters in Robin Hood myth reformed in time

indicators.note: Something reformed has been built again in a new shape, so those letters are set down in a different order.
The original character of a word is the letter it starts with, so only the initials of the words that follow are collected.

parts.note: the opening letters of ROBIN and HOOD, which stay as they are
the four letters of MYTH rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: The Robin Hood legend retold for a modern audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Original characters in Robin Hood myth' reads as one phrase and only covers the outlaw's name; the myth itself is fodder. Time is the musician's sense, the beat a drummer keeps.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer keeping time is keeping the rhythm, the beat a piece of music moves to.
